questions.q: What is an example of an "incomplete rules" error during Create Accounting?
options: A supplier record with a missing phone number
An account rule or journal line rule that has no matching condition for the data present on a specific real transaction
A journal entry that is perfectly balanced
A ledger with too many currencies
questions.explain: Incomplete rules occur when no condition in a rule matches a real transaction's data, even if the rule passed validation earlier.

questions.q: What is the correct way to fix an error on a journal entry that is still in Draft mode?
options: Create a reversal entry against it
It cannot be fixed; Draft entries are permanent
Manually edit the Draft entry's lines directly in the database
Correct the underlying issue (rule, mapping set, or account) and simply re-run Create Accounting in Draft mode
questions.explain: Draft entries can be safely re-created; fixing the root cause and re-running Draft mode replaces the old draft cleanly.

questions.q: Why can't a Final subledger journal entry simply be deleted or silently altered when it's wrong?
options: Final entries do not actually exist in the database
Deleting or silently altering it would break the permanent audit trail that accounting systems depend on
There is no technical reason; it's just a convention nobody follows
Final entries automatically self-correct over time
questions.explain: Preserving the audit trail requires that a Final entry's history remain visible; correction is done through reversal, not deletion.

questions.q: What is the standard correction technique for a Final entry that was accounted incorrectly?
options: Ignore it and hope nobody notices
Change the ledger's Chart of Accounts
Delete the General Ledger journal that resulted from it
Create an offsetting reversal entry to cancel the original, followed by a new, correct entry
questions.explain: Reversal creates an offsetting entry that cancels the original's net effect while preserving the full history of what happened.

questions.q: Why does this lesson distinguish between fixing a single transaction and fixing a rule?
options: There is no meaningful distinction; both are handled identically
Because rules can never be the cause of an accounting error
Because a flawed rule likely affected every transaction that matched its conditions, not just the one a reviewer happened to notice first
Because only Final entries can ever be affected by a rule problem
questions.explain: If the root cause is a rule rather than bad data on one transaction, every other transaction affected by that same rule likely needs correction too.
